newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The rand finished over a cent weaker in thin dealings on Friday depressed by a large import order in the market, dealers said.
"There was a big import order below the 4.53 level that hit the market just before noon," a dealer said.
"It was just one big shove that took us weaker and then we got stuck because of the small volumes going through," he added.
The local unit, which ended at 4.5350/5400 from a 4.5250/5300 close on Thursday, spent most of the afternoon hovering above the 4.5350 level. It touched a worst level of 4.5375 on the day.
"It got through 4.53 (on the upside) quite easily. The next big levels are 4.54 and 4.55," another dealer said.
Traders said exporters had been scarce, and looked to be waiting for the rand to go to weaker levels.
A lot of players spent the day squaring positions ahead of the weekend.
The rand was seen trading in a 4.50-4.54 range next week, although it could easily break out of this band, dealers said.
"It has been such a choppy week that it is difficult to predict where the rand is going. If it breaks out of the range it could run. There are stop loss levels on either side," a trader said.
Against the crosses the local unit weakened to last trade at 7.0997/7.1074 from 7.0848/0967 against sterling late on Wednesday and was at 0.3367/3372 from 0.3379/3384 marks previously.
Key long bonds were soft in late afternoon trade on a weaker and volatile rand, but were helped off their day's worst levels by gains on the U.S. bond market, dealers said.
The key R150 bond was at 15.28 pct from 15.210 at 1400 GMT on Thursday, after hitting a weakest level of 15.335 earlier in the day.
"Until the rand stabilises or strengthens, the market is not going to go anywhere in a hurry," a bond dealer said.
"We have had great support from offshore bond markets," he said referring to the U.S. 30-year Treasury bond which rallied on Friday following the release of September non-farm payrolls.
Figures showed a drop of 40,000 jobs against a forecast rise of 166,000 prompting analysts to predict the Federal Reserve is likely to keep interest rates steady in the near future.
Dealers said some offshore buying of local bonds was evident after the release of the U.S. data, but this was met by selling by local institutions.
They said the announcement that the Reserve Bank would be releasing September gold and foreign exchange reserve figures on Friday instead of Monday had not affected the market.
"There are so few people around because of a Golf Day and most people spent the day squaring positions," one said.

Analysts polled by Reuters said gross reserves would come in at 10.06 billion rand in September from 10.08 billion in August. The average forecast was drawn from a range of 9.8 billion rand to 10.5 billion rand.
Dealers said direction on the bond market next week would be determined by the rand's movements.
"If you took a graph of the R150 and a graph of the rand, you can see how closely their movements match," according to one.
Bond Exchange figures show foreigners bought a net 188.68 million rand worth of South African bonds on Thursday after buying a net 353.96 million rand on Wednesday, the Bond Exchange said.
Nominal cumulative volumes amounted to 35.39 billion rand on Thursday -- a settlement day -- from 5.35 billion rand on Wednesday.
On the money market, three-month NCDs were steady at between 15.75 and 15.95 percent, while 90-day BAs were unchanged in a 15.20-15.35 percent band.
The daily shortage remained above nine billion rand edging slightly lower to 9.425 billion rand on Thursday from 9.936 billion rand on Wednesday.
-- Nicole Mordant, Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482 1003
